How is pricing calculated for the paid plans? If you upgrade your workspace to one of the paid plans, you will be charged a fee per member. Guests are free of charge – but they can only access individual pages they are invited to. In other words, guests won’t be able to see all the team pages under the `Teamspaces` section in the left sidebar.

How are paid seats counted? A paid seat can be thought of as a license for one member to use your Notion workspace. Workspace owners can view the total paid seat count for their workspace by going to `Settings & members` > `Billing` . Once you have added a paid seat, you will keep it for the duration of your billing period. When your billing cycle renews, either monthly or annually, you will be charged for your plan amount multiplied by the number of members in your workspace, plus any prorated charges for new paid seats added in the past month. Your number of paid seats will be recalculated at each renewal to match the number of members present in the workspace.

excerpts: Freemium pricing means offering a product or service for free at the entry level, with the option of paid upgrades for users who want more premium features, usage, or control.
This strategy, which eliminates the barrier to entry, is built on the idea that once people try something useful, some of them will stick around and pay for the full version.
The free tier isn’t a trial.
Usually, it remains free forever.
The model works by splitting a product into tiers:
**Free:** This tier is functional but limited. This might mean usage caps, ads, fewer features, or no support.
**Paid:** This tier adds power and can include additional features such as more storage, access to advanced tools, collaboration features, and faster support.
The free version should solve a real need.
The paid version should solve it better, faster, or at scale.
The focus of freemium is what features you reserve for paying customers.
That could involve usage limits (e.g., storage, seats, projects), feature access (e.g., automation, integrations, admin controls), or experience upgrades (e.g., speed, support, customization).
If everyone needs a feature, it probably belongs in the free plan.
If only power users need it, that’s your upgrade lever.
Make the upgrade path obvious
People upgrade when the value gap between what they have and what they want becomes undeniable.

Build your product to create natural pressure: **Set a usage cap for customers to hit:** “You’ve completed your 10 free projects.” **Try a gated feature:** “Pro feature—upgrade to use.” **Harness a bottleneck:** “Add teammates—starts at $X per month.”

Your free plan has to prove that the product is worth a user’s time. That means putting your core value—the job the product performs—front and center in the free tier. If people don’t experience the payoff, they’ll leave before you ever get the chance to convert them.

Sign-ups are meaningless if people never activate. Use your onboarding to get users to that first “aha” moment quickly or whatever action correlates with their long-term use of your product. That might be importing data, completing a workflow, or hitting a daily usage threshold. The faster someone finds value, the more likely they are to stick around and eventually pay.
The free version should solve a real need. The paid version should solve it better, faster, or at scale.
If everyone needs a feature, it probably belongs in the free plan. If only power users need it, that’s your upgrade lever.

Draw a smart line between free and paid The focus of freemium is what features you reserve for paying customers. That could involve usage limits (e.g., storage, seats, projects), feature access (e.g., automation, integrations, admin controls), or experience upgrades (e.g., speed, support, customization).

Make the upgrade path obvious People upgrade when the value gap between what they have and what they want becomes undeniable. Build your product to create natural pressure: **Set a usage cap for customers to hit:** “You’ve completed your 10 free projects.” **Try a gated feature:** “Pro feature—upgrade to use.” **Harness a bottleneck:** “Add teammates—starts at $X per month.”
Make the upgrade path obvious People upgrade when the value gap between what they have and what they want becomes undeniable. Build your product to create natural pressure:

The model works by splitting a product into tiers: **Free:** This tier is functional but limited. This might mean usage caps, ads, fewer features, or no support. **Paid:** This tier adds power and can include additional features such as more storage, access to advanced tools, collaboration features, and faster support.
Freemium hinges on giving away the exact right amount: enough to show value, but not so much that users never need to upgrade.

Freemium pricing sounds simple: you give away part of your product for free and charge for the rest. But in practice, it’s one of the hardest pricing models to get right. If you give away too much, users don’t upgrade. If you give away too little, they don’t stick around long enough to care about your product.

|Monetization and product |Builds brand visibility and creates natural upsell paths for advanced features |Risk of cannibalizing paid tiers if the free product is overly generous | |Operations and cost |Generates rich user data to guide product development and feature improvements |Serves nonpaying users with real infrastructure, support, and operational costs | |Retention and fit |Establishes daily habits and trust before asking for a financial commitment |Higher initial churn from low-intent users; unsustainable for high-marginal-cost products |

The freemium business model defers immediate revenue in exchange for rapid, frictionless user acquisition. Companies that use it are betting that a subset of free users will eventually convert into paying customers. While it serves as a powerful growth engine, businesses will need to carefully manage feature limits, infrastructure costs, and conversion rates.

High churn rates Free users are generally less invested and more likely to drop off. A large portion will sign up, then vanish. That’s expected. But if most customers are lost to [churn](https://stripe.com/resources/more/customer-churn-rates-101) before they ever hit a paywall, that’s a problem. You need solid onboarding, fast time to value, and enough stickiness to retain some people long enough to convert.

How do you design a successful freemium pricing model? To make freemium work, your product must strike a balance: free enough to attract and retain subscribers, constrained enough to drive upgrades, and efficient enough to scale without draining your resources. Here’s what that takes.

Start with your core value Your free plan has to prove that the product is worth a user’s time. That means putting your core value—the job the product performs—front and center in the free tier. If people don’t experience the payoff, they’ll leave before you ever get the chance to convert them.

Know your provider costs Free users aren’t free to you. If the cost to acquire, support, and keep them is too high relative to their conversion potential, your [burn rate](https://stripe.com/resources/more/what-is-burn-rate-what-startups-need-to-know-about-this-key-metric) will be unsustainable. Run the numbers. Know what each user costs, how much value they’re likely to generate, and how long it takes for the average paid user to pay back their acquisition and support costs. Your infrastructure, support model, and margin need to scale with usage rather than fight it.

Keep improving The line between free and paid isn’t permanent. As your product develops, your [pricing model](https://stripe.com/resources/more/pricing-models-explained-types-of-pricing-models-and-when-to-use-them) should too. The best freemium models are responsive, so tweak limits, adjust pricing, and add or remove upgrade gates. Pay attention to behavior indicators: where people are getting stuck, what features trigger upgrades, and who’s leaving and why.

The free product must be good enough to entice people, but also incomplete so it creates a natural pull towards the paid version. The line between the two is easy to misjudge and difficult to alter once people are used to getting something for nothing. The right fit If your product has high marginal costs (e.g., anything that requires human labor, difficult operations, expensive computing power), freemium might be unsustainable. The same goes for products that serve a very specific audience or have a high delivery cost. High churn rates Free users are generally less invested and more likely to drop off. A large portion will sign up, then vanish. That’s expected. But if most customers are lost to [churn](https://stripe.com/resources/more/customer-churn-rates-101) before they ever hit a paywall, that’s a problem. You need solid onboarding, fast time to value, and enough stickiness to retain some people long enough to convert. Involved day-to-day work Running a freemium business means managing two sets of users (free and paid) with different needs, limits, and expectations. That affects product decisions, pricing logic, support ops, [billing](https://stripe.com/resources/more/billing-models-types-and-their-challenges) infrastructure, and analytics. Freemium is a trade-off. You’re deferring revenue in exchange for reach, betting that enough people will eventually upgrade.

excerpts: A **subscription** is the recurring relationship between a customer and one of your [products](/docs/features/products).
It's created automatically whenever a customer checks out a product that has a recurring price, and it keeps generating orders on each renewal until the customer or you decide to end it.

**A customer subscribes.** When a customer completes a [checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session) for a product that has a recurring price, Polar creates a `subscription` and the first [order](/docs/features/orders).

**Polar renews it automatically.** At the end of each billing period, Polar advances the subscription to the next cycle and creates a new order, then attempts to charge the customer's default payment method. If the payment fails, the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar runs an automated [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments).

**Benefits stay in sync.** As long as the subscription is active or trialing, the customer keeps access to all the [benefits](/docs/features/benefits/introduction) attached to the product. When the subscription ends, those benefits are revoked.

Subscriptions > Recurring revenue on top of your products. A **subscription** is the recurring relationship between a customer and one of your [products](/docs/features/products). It's created automatically whenever a customer checks out a product that has a recurring price, and it keeps generating orders on each renewal until the customer or you decide to end it. How subscriptions work **A customer subscribes.** When a customer completes a [checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session) for a product that has a recurring price, Polar creates a `subscription` and the first [order](/docs/features/orders). **Polar renews it automatically.** At the end of each billing period, Polar advances the subscription to the next cycle and creates a new order, then attempts to charge the customer's default payment method. If the payment fails, the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar runs an automated [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments). **Benefits stay in sync.** As long as the subscription is active or trialing, the customer keeps access to all the [benefits](/docs/features/benefits/introduction) attached to the product. When the subscription ends, those benefits are revoked. **Customers self-serve from the portal.** The [Customer Portal](/docs/features/customer-portal/introduction) lets customers update their payment method, download invoices, cancel, and — if you allow it — change plans or manage seats. Recurring pricing Subscriptions are driven entirely by the way you price the underlying product. Recurring pricing is configured when you [create a product](/docs/features/products#pricing): **Billing interval.** Daily, weekly, monthly or yearly. **Interval count.** The number of units per cycle. Setting this to `2` with a `month` interval gives you "every 2 months". **Pricing type.** Fixed, pay-what-you-want, or free. Free recurring products are still modeled as subscriptions — they just never generate a payment. **Currency.** A product can have prices in multiple currencies; the subscription locks in the currency used at checkout. <Note> The billing interval and pricing type are fixed once a product is created. If you need a different interval (for example, a yearly plan next to a monthly one), create a separate product and show both at checkout. See [Products → Variants](/docs/features/products#variants). </Note> Renewal reminders For subscriptions on long billing cycles — six months or more — Polar emails the customer **7 days before the renewal date** to let them know an upcoming charge is coming. This helps with regulations (like the EU's Consumer Rights Directive) that require advance notice on long-interval renewals, and avoids surprise charges that often end in chargebacks. The threshold is six months, however it is expressed: yearly plans, monthly plans with an interval of 6 or more, weekly plans of 25 or more, and daily plans of 180 or more all get the reminder. Reminders are skipped for free subscriptions and for subscriptions already scheduled to cancel at period end. You can turn renewal reminders off under [**Settings → Customer notifications**](https://polar.sh/to/dashboard/settings) if you prefer to handle that communication yourself. Cancellation A subscription can end in one of two ways, both available to you and your customers: **Cancel at period end** — the subscription keeps working until `current_period_end`, then transitions to `canceled`. You can reverse this (uncancel) until the end date is reached. **Revoke immediately** — the subscription moves to `canceled` right away and benefits are revoked. This is irreversible. See [Managing subscriptions](/docs/features/subscriptions/manage) for how to perform these actions and everything else merchants can do from the dashboard or the API. Creating subscriptions There are two ways a subscription can come into existence: **Through checkout.** The default. Works for any paid recurring product. See [Checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session). **Through the API, for free recurring products only.** You can call [Create Subscription](/docs/api-reference/subscriptions/create-subscription) to subscribe an existing customer to a free product — no order, no email, no charge. This is useful for freemium onboarding flows where you want every signup to have a subscription tied to it from day one. Paid products always go through checkout so that Polar can collect and validate the payment method. Next steps <CardGroup cols={2}> <Card title="Managing subscriptions" icon="sliders" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/manage"> Change plans, seats, trials, billing dates, cancel or revoke — from the dashboard or the API. </Card> <Card title="Proration" icon="scale-balanced" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/proration"> Control how the price difference is handled when a subscription is upgraded or downgraded. </Card> <Card title="Recovering failed payments" icon="credit-card" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments"> How Polar retries failed renewals and when benefits are revoked. </Card> <Card title="Subscriptions API" icon="code" href="/docs/api-reference/subscriptions/list-subscriptions"> List, create, update, and revoke subscriptions programmatically. </Card> </CardGroup> FAQ <AccordionGroup> <Accordion title="What's the difference between a subscription and a product?"> A product is the thing you're selling — name, description, benefits, pricing. A subscription is one specific customer's ongoing relationship with that product. Polar treats one-time purchases and recurring subscriptions as the same kind of object (both are "products"); the only difference is whether the price is recurring. See [Products](/docs/features/products) for the full model. </Accordion> <Accordion title="Can a customer have more than one active subscription?"> By default, no — a customer can only have one active subscription per organization at a time. This keeps the common case simple. If your product genuinely needs multiple parallel subscriptions per customer, you can opt in under **Organization Settings → Subscriptions** by toggling on **Allow multiple subscriptions**. </Accordion> <Accordion title="When is a customer actually charged?"> At the end of each billing cycle. When a subscription renews, Polar advances the cycle, creates a new order with tax and any applicable discount, and charges the customer's default payment method. If you update the price on a product, the change applies only to **new** subscriptions. To move an existing subscriber to different pricing, either create a new product and run an [update to switch them to it](/docs/features/subscriptions/manage#change-the-plan), or ask them to change plans themselves from the Customer Portal. </Accordion> <Accordion title="What happens to benefits when a subscription is canceled?"> Benefits are tied to the subscription's status, not to the cancellation action itself: If you **cancel at period end**, the customer keeps their benefits until `current_period_end` — they paid for that period. **How does Miro's pricing work?** Miro plans are priced per seat. On the Free plan, all users are free. If you're on a Starter or Business plan, you're charged for every member added to your workspace. Assessment rationale:
- The field description appears to require a comprehensive packaging recommendation for agency OS pricing and economics, including ICPs, payer, per-seat vs workspace vs usage-based models, freemium/gated features, and cross-product packaging implications. 
- The provided field_answer lists a multi-product pricing snapshot (Productive, Scoro, AgencyAnalytics, Accelo) focusing on who pays (ICP) and some price points / seat requirements, but it does not fully cover all requested aspects (e.g., detailed per-seat vs workspace vs usage-based metering across all modules, freemium gates, exact packaging recommendations, cross-product SKU structuring, and the broader competitive context of Polar.sh vs Stripe, etc.). 
- Therefore, completeness should be false because it does not address all elements implied by the field description and user query, though it is partially supported by excerpts showing price/ICP data for several vendors.
- Excerpts appear to support the field answer’s specific prices and ICP payer notes for the included products, but not the full breadth of requested analysis and packaging guidance.
- Confidence in the field answer being fully complete is low; it is partial and requires expansion to meet the field description fully.

- The field_description asks for a packaging recommendation with price bands, what to leave free, what to gate, and what to meter, focusing on AI packaging in a hybrid product ecosystem and including multiple vendors (Notion, Motion, Linear, Cursor, Miro, Craft, Heptabase, Figma, Craft, etc.). It also asks to cover ICPs, billing models (per-seat/workspace/usage-based credits), freemium gates, viability of a $19/mo all-in Pro with specific quotas, and common entitlement pitfalls.
- The provided field_answer includes a cross-vendor summary of AI packaging options with concrete pricing scaffolds (Notion credits, Motion credits per seat, Linear per-user pricing with AI workflows, Cursor usage-based pricing, Miro AI credits pooled per org, Craft/pricing, Heptabase tiers with AI credits, Craft pricing, etc.), as well as qualitative guidance on budgeting, shared credit pools, and when to meter vs. queue unlimited usage.
- It also discusses the differences in AI credit UX models (shared pool vs per-seat quota vs on-demand arrears) and highlights entitlements pitfalls, matching the field_description’s requirement to propose a structured packaging approach.
- Excerpt evidence supports the inclusion of the various pricing/credits mechanisms and the observed tradeoffs between different models, so the answer is aligned with the excerpts.
- Therefore, completeness is judged true (covers required aspects) and supportability is true (excerpts back the key points).

excerpts: Freemium pricing means offering a product or service for free at the entry level, with the option of paid upgrades for users who want more premium features, usage, or control.
This strategy, which eliminates the barrier to entry, is built on the idea that once people try something useful, some of them will stick around and pay for the full version.
The free tier isn’t a trial.
Usually, it remains free forever.
The model works by splitting a product into tiers:
**Free:** This tier is functional but limited. This might mean usage caps, ads, fewer features, or no support.
**Paid:** This tier adds power and can include additional features such as more storage, access to advanced tools, collaboration features, and faster support.
The free version should solve a real need.
The paid version should solve it better, faster, or at scale.
The focus of freemium is what features you reserve for paying customers.
That could involve usage limits (e.g., storage, seats, projects), feature access (e.g., automation, integrations, admin controls), or experience upgrades (e.g., speed, support, customization).
If everyone needs a feature, it probably belongs in the free plan.
If only power users need it, that’s your upgrade lever.
Make the upgrade path obvious
People upgrade when the value gap between what they have and what they want becomes undeniable.

Build your product to create natural pressure: **Set a usage cap for customers to hit:** “You’ve completed your 10 free projects.” **Try a gated feature:** “Pro feature—upgrade to use.” **Harness a bottleneck:** “Add teammates—starts at $X per month.”

Your free plan has to prove that the product is worth a user’s time. That means putting your core value—the job the product performs—front and center in the free tier. If people don’t experience the payoff, they’ll leave before you ever get the chance to convert them.

Sign-ups are meaningless if people never activate. Use your onboarding to get users to that first “aha” moment quickly or whatever action correlates with their long-term use of your product. That might be importing data, completing a workflow, or hitting a daily usage threshold. The faster someone finds value, the more likely they are to stick around and eventually pay.
The free version should solve a real need. The paid version should solve it better, faster, or at scale.
If everyone needs a feature, it probably belongs in the free plan. If only power users need it, that’s your upgrade lever.

Draw a smart line between free and paid The focus of freemium is what features you reserve for paying customers. That could involve usage limits (e.g., storage, seats, projects), feature access (e.g., automation, integrations, admin controls), or experience upgrades (e.g., speed, support, customization).

Make the upgrade path obvious People upgrade when the value gap between what they have and what they want becomes undeniable. Build your product to create natural pressure: **Set a usage cap for customers to hit:** “You’ve completed your 10 free projects.” **Try a gated feature:** “Pro feature—upgrade to use.” **Harness a bottleneck:** “Add teammates—starts at $X per month.”
Make the upgrade path obvious People upgrade when the value gap between what they have and what they want becomes undeniable. Build your product to create natural pressure:

The model works by splitting a product into tiers: **Free:** This tier is functional but limited. This might mean usage caps, ads, fewer features, or no support. **Paid:** This tier adds power and can include additional features such as more storage, access to advanced tools, collaboration features, and faster support.
Freemium hinges on giving away the exact right amount: enough to show value, but not so much that users never need to upgrade.

Freemium pricing sounds simple: you give away part of your product for free and charge for the rest. But in practice, it’s one of the hardest pricing models to get right. If you give away too much, users don’t upgrade. If you give away too little, they don’t stick around long enough to care about your product.

|Monetization and product |Builds brand visibility and creates natural upsell paths for advanced features |Risk of cannibalizing paid tiers if the free product is overly generous | |Operations and cost |Generates rich user data to guide product development and feature improvements |Serves nonpaying users with real infrastructure, support, and operational costs | |Retention and fit |Establishes daily habits and trust before asking for a financial commitment |Higher initial churn from low-intent users; unsustainable for high-marginal-cost products |

The freemium business model defers immediate revenue in exchange for rapid, frictionless user acquisition. Companies that use it are betting that a subset of free users will eventually convert into paying customers. While it serves as a powerful growth engine, businesses will need to carefully manage feature limits, infrastructure costs, and conversion rates.

High churn rates Free users are generally less invested and more likely to drop off. A large portion will sign up, then vanish. That’s expected. But if most customers are lost to [churn](https://stripe.com/resources/more/customer-churn-rates-101) before they ever hit a paywall, that’s a problem. You need solid onboarding, fast time to value, and enough stickiness to retain some people long enough to convert.

How do you design a successful freemium pricing model? To make freemium work, your product must strike a balance: free enough to attract and retain subscribers, constrained enough to drive upgrades, and efficient enough to scale without draining your resources. Here’s what that takes.

Start with your core value Your free plan has to prove that the product is worth a user’s time. That means putting your core value—the job the product performs—front and center in the free tier. If people don’t experience the payoff, they’ll leave before you ever get the chance to convert them.

Know your provider costs Free users aren’t free to you. If the cost to acquire, support, and keep them is too high relative to their conversion potential, your [burn rate](https://stripe.com/resources/more/what-is-burn-rate-what-startups-need-to-know-about-this-key-metric) will be unsustainable. Run the numbers. Know what each user costs, how much value they’re likely to generate, and how long it takes for the average paid user to pay back their acquisition and support costs. Your infrastructure, support model, and margin need to scale with usage rather than fight it.

Keep improving The line between free and paid isn’t permanent. As your product develops, your [pricing model](https://stripe.com/resources/more/pricing-models-explained-types-of-pricing-models-and-when-to-use-them) should too. The best freemium models are responsive, so tweak limits, adjust pricing, and add or remove upgrade gates. Pay attention to behavior indicators: where people are getting stuck, what features trigger upgrades, and who’s leaving and why.

The free product must be good enough to entice people, but also incomplete so it creates a natural pull towards the paid version. The line between the two is easy to misjudge and difficult to alter once people are used to getting something for nothing. The right fit If your product has high marginal costs (e.g., anything that requires human labor, difficult operations, expensive computing power), freemium might be unsustainable. The same goes for products that serve a very specific audience or have a high delivery cost. High churn rates Free users are generally less invested and more likely to drop off. A large portion will sign up, then vanish. That’s expected. But if most customers are lost to [churn](https://stripe.com/resources/more/customer-churn-rates-101) before they ever hit a paywall, that’s a problem. You need solid onboarding, fast time to value, and enough stickiness to retain some people long enough to convert. Involved day-to-day work Running a freemium business means managing two sets of users (free and paid) with different needs, limits, and expectations. That affects product decisions, pricing logic, support ops, [billing](https://stripe.com/resources/more/billing-models-types-and-their-challenges) infrastructure, and analytics. Freemium is a trade-off. You’re deferring revenue in exchange for reach, betting that enough people will eventually upgrade.

excerpts: A **subscription** is the recurring relationship between a customer and one of your [products](/docs/features/products).
It's created automatically whenever a customer checks out a product that has a recurring price, and it keeps generating orders on each renewal until the customer or you decide to end it.

**A customer subscribes.** When a customer completes a [checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session) for a product that has a recurring price, Polar creates a `subscription` and the first [order](/docs/features/orders).

**Polar renews it automatically.** At the end of each billing period, Polar advances the subscription to the next cycle and creates a new order, then attempts to charge the customer's default payment method. If the payment fails, the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar runs an automated [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments).

**Benefits stay in sync.** As long as the subscription is active or trialing, the customer keeps access to all the [benefits](/docs/features/benefits/introduction) attached to the product. When the subscription ends, those benefits are revoked.

Subscriptions > Recurring revenue on top of your products. A **subscription** is the recurring relationship between a customer and one of your [products](/docs/features/products). It's created automatically whenever a customer checks out a product that has a recurring price, and it keeps generating orders on each renewal until the customer or you decide to end it. How subscriptions work **A customer subscribes.** When a customer completes a [checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session) for a product that has a recurring price, Polar creates a `subscription` and the first [order](/docs/features/orders). **Polar renews it automatically.** At the end of each billing period, Polar advances the subscription to the next cycle and creates a new order, then attempts to charge the customer's default payment method. If the payment fails, the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar runs an automated [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments). **Benefits stay in sync.** As long as the subscription is active or trialing, the customer keeps access to all the [benefits](/docs/features/benefits/introduction) attached to the product. When the subscription ends, those benefits are revoked. **Customers self-serve from the portal.** The [Customer Portal](/docs/features/customer-portal/introduction) lets customers update their payment method, download invoices, cancel, and — if you allow it — change plans or manage seats. Recurring pricing Subscriptions are driven entirely by the way you price the underlying product. Recurring pricing is configured when you [create a product](/docs/features/products#pricing): **Billing interval.** Daily, weekly, monthly or yearly. **Interval count.** The number of units per cycle. Setting this to `2` with a `month` interval gives you "every 2 months". **Pricing type.** Fixed, pay-what-you-want, or free. Free recurring products are still modeled as subscriptions — they just never generate a payment. **Currency.** A product can have prices in multiple currencies; the subscription locks in the currency used at checkout. <Note> The billing interval and pricing type are fixed once a product is created. If you need a different interval (for example, a yearly plan next to a monthly one), create a separate product and show both at checkout. See [Products → Variants](/docs/features/products#variants). </Note> Renewal reminders For subscriptions on long billing cycles — six months or more — Polar emails the customer **7 days before the renewal date** to let them know an upcoming charge is coming. This helps with regulations (like the EU's Consumer Rights Directive) that require advance notice on long-interval renewals, and avoids surprise charges that often end in chargebacks. The threshold is six months, however it is expressed: yearly plans, monthly plans with an interval of 6 or more, weekly plans of 25 or more, and daily plans of 180 or more all get the reminder. Reminders are skipped for free subscriptions and for subscriptions already scheduled to cancel at period end. You can turn renewal reminders off under [**Settings → Customer notifications**](https://polar.sh/to/dashboard/settings) if you prefer to handle that communication yourself. Cancellation A subscription can end in one of two ways, both available to you and your customers: **Cancel at period end** — the subscription keeps working until `current_period_end`, then transitions to `canceled`. You can reverse this (uncancel) until the end date is reached. **Revoke immediately** — the subscription moves to `canceled` right away and benefits are revoked. This is irreversible. See [Managing subscriptions](/docs/features/subscriptions/manage) for how to perform these actions and everything else merchants can do from the dashboard or the API. Creating subscriptions There are two ways a subscription can come into existence: **Through checkout.** The default. Works for any paid recurring product. See [Checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session). **Through the API, for free recurring products only.** You can call [Create Subscription](/docs/api-reference/subscriptions/create-subscription) to subscribe an existing customer to a free product — no order, no email, no charge. This is useful for freemium onboarding flows where you want every signup to have a subscription tied to it from day one. Paid products always go through checkout so that Polar can collect and validate the payment method. Next steps <CardGroup cols={2}> <Card title="Managing subscriptions" icon="sliders" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/manage"> Change plans, seats, trials, billing dates, cancel or revoke — from the dashboard or the API. </Card> <Card title="Proration" icon="scale-balanced" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/proration"> Control how the price difference is handled when a subscription is upgraded or downgraded. </Card> <Card title="Recovering failed payments" icon="credit-card" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments"> How Polar retries failed renewals and when benefits are revoked. </Card> <Card title="Subscriptions API" icon="code" href="/docs/api-reference/subscriptions/list-subscriptions"> List, create, update, and revoke subscriptions programmatically. </Card> </CardGroup> FAQ <AccordionGroup> <Accordion title="What's the difference between a subscription and a product?"> A product is the thing you're selling — name, description, benefits, pricing. A subscription is one specific customer's ongoing relationship with that product. Polar treats one-time purchases and recurring subscriptions as the same kind of object (both are "products"); the only difference is whether the price is recurring. See [Products](/docs/features/products) for the full model. </Accordion> <Accordion title="Can a customer have more than one active subscription?"> By default, no — a customer can only have one active subscription per organization at a time. This keeps the common case simple. If your product genuinely needs multiple parallel subscriptions per customer, you can opt in under **Organization Settings → Subscriptions** by toggling on **Allow multiple subscriptions**. </Accordion> <Accordion title="When is a customer actually charged?"> At the end of each billing cycle. When a subscription renews, Polar advances the cycle, creates a new order with tax and any applicable discount, and charges the customer's default payment method. If the charge fails the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar starts the [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments). The first charge happens at checkout (or when the [trial](/docs/features/subscriptions/trials) ends, if one is configured). </Accordion> <Accordion title="Can I change the price of an existing subscription?"> Not the amount on an existing subscription directly — subscriptions lock in the price they were created with so existing subscribers aren't surprised by changes. If you update the price on a product, the change applies only to **new** subscriptions. To move an existing subscriber to different pricing, either create a new product and run an [update to switch them to it](/docs/features/subscriptions/manage#change-the-plan), or ask them to change plans themselves from the Customer Portal. </Accordion> <Accordion title="What happens to benefits when a subscription is canceled?"> Benefits are tied to the subscription's status, not to the cancellation action itself: If you **cancel at period end**, the customer keeps their benefits until `current_period_end` — they paid for that period. Polar is then able to compute the usage over time, both globally and per customer.
A filter is a set of clauses that are combined using conjunctions. They're used to filter events that you've ingested into Polar.

Conjunctions A conjunction is a logical operator that combines two or more clauses. **and** — All clauses must be true for the event to be included. **or** — At least one clause must be true for the event to be included. Aggregation The aggregation is the function that is used to aggregate the events that match the filter. For example, if you want to count the number of events that match the filter, you can use the **Count** aggregation. If you want to sum the value of a metadata field, you can use the **Sum** aggregation. **Count** — Counts the number of events that match the filter. **Sum** — Sums the value of a property.

OpenRouter automatically returns detailed usage information with every response, including: Prompt and completion token counts using the model's native tokenizer Cost in credits Reasoning token counts (if applicable) Cached token counts (if available) This information is included in the last SSE message for streaming responses, or in the complete response for non-streaming requests. No additional parameters are required. <Note> **Deprecated Parameters** The `usage: { include: true }` and `stream_options: { include_usage: true }` parameters are deprecated and have no effect. Full usage details are now always included automatically in every response. </Note> Response Format Every response includes a `usage` object with detailed token information: ```json lines theme={null} { "object": "chat.completion.chunk", "usage": { "completion_tokens": 2, "completion_tokens_details": { "reasoning_tokens": 0 }, "cost": 0.95, "cost_details": { "upstream_inference_cost": 19 }, "prompt_tokens": 194, "prompt_tokens_details": { "cached_tokens": 0, "cache_write_tokens": 100, "audio_tokens": 0 }, "total_tokens": 196 } } ``` `cached_tokens` is the number of tokens that were *read* from the cache. `cache_write_tokens` is the number of tokens that were *written* to the cache (only returned for models with explicit caching and cache write pricing). excerpts: Credit limits govern how much you can spend.
They come from two places:

**Account balance**, your available credits across the account. If your account has a negative credit balance, you may see <StatusCode code={HTTPStatus.S402_Payment_Required} /> errors, including for free models. Adding credits to put your balance above zero allows you to use those models again.

**Per-key credit limits**, an optional spending cap configured on an individual API key. The `limit`, `limit_reset`, and `limit_remaining` fields in the `GET /api/v1/key` response above describe this cap and how much of it remains.

```typescript title="TypeScript" expandable lines theme={null} type Key = { data: { label: string; limit: number | null; // Credit limit for the key, or null if unlimited limit_reset: string | null; // Type of limit reset for the key, or null if never resets limit_remaining: number | null; // Remaining credits for the key, or null if unlimited include_byok_in_limit: boolean; // Whether to include external BYOK usage in the credit limit usage: number; // Number of credits used (all time) usage_daily: number; // Number of credits used (current UTC day) usage_weekly: number; // ... (current UTC week, starting Monday) usage_monthly: number; // ... (current UTC month)
byok_usage: number; // Same for external BYOK usage byok_usage_daily: number; byok_usage_weekly: number; byok_usage_monthly: number;
To check the rate limit or credits left on an API key, make a GET request to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/key`.
**Monitor proactively.** Call `GET /api/v1/key` as shown above to track `limit_remaining` and usage before requests start failing.
The `free_model_daily_requests` field in the `GET /api/v1/key` response above reports the daily counter and ceiling that gate your free-model requests when these limits apply to your account.
Rate limits govern how many requests you can make.

**Free usage limits**: If you're using a free model variant (with an ID ending in {sep}{Variant.Free}), the following limits apply: | Credits purchased (all time) | Requests per minute | Requests per day | | Less than {FREE_MODEL_CREDITS_THRESHOLD} | {FREE_MODEL_RATE_LIMIT_RPM} | {FREE_MODEL_NO_CREDITS_RPD} | | At least {FREE_MODEL_CREDITS_THRESHOLD} | {FREE_MODEL_RATE_LIMIT_RPM} | {FREE_MODEL_HAS_CREDITS_RPD} |
**DDoS protection**: Cloudflare's DDoS protection will block requests that dramatically exceed reasonable usage.
**Retry with exponential backoff.** Rate limits are transient; wait and retry rather than immediately re-sending. Honor the `Retry-After` header when present.
**On free variants**, purchase at least {FREE_MODEL_CREDITS_THRESHOLD} credits to raise your daily limit, or switch to the paid variant of the model, which has no platform-level request cap.

**For provider-side limits**, add [fallback models](/docs/guides/routing/model-fallbacks) or relax [provider routing preferences](/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection) so more providers are eligible to serve the request.

Accounts and endpoints exempt from free-model limits, and BYOK requests, are not gated by it, so `remaining` reflects the tier policy rather than an enforced ceiling for them. The per-minute limit is not reported there. The `limit` tier is selected by all-time credits purchased, independently of `is_free_tier`. To absorb rounding and top-up fees, the higher daily ceiling is granted starting one credit below the table's threshold (currently {FREE_MODEL_CREDITS_THRESHOLD - 1} credits); an account that has purchased fewer credits than that reports `is_free_tier: false` together with the lower daily ceiling. **DDoS protection**: Cloudflare's DDoS protection will block requests that dramatically exceed reasonable usage. Handling 429 errors Requests rejected with fail with a standard [error response](/docs/api_reference/errors-and-debugging): ```json lines theme={null} { "error": { "code": 429, "message": "Rate limit exceeded", "metadata": { "error_type": "rate_limit_exceeded" } } } ``` A error can come from two places: **OpenRouter**, when you hit one of the platform limits above (free-model requests per minute or per day, or DDoS protection). **The upstream provider**, when the provider serving your request is rate limiting or at capacity. In this case `error.metadata.provider_code` carries the provider's original error code when available, and [fallback routing](/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection) retries other providers for the same model automatically before the error reaches you. You can also specify [fallback models](/docs/guides/routing/model-fallbacks) to try a different model when all providers for the first are exhausted. Successful inference responses do not include `X-RateLimit-*` headers. When OpenRouter itself returns a error for a platform limit, the error response carries `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers describing the limit that was hit. When every attempted provider returned a retry hint, the error response also carries a `Retry-After` header. To monitor your remaining quota before hitting a limit, call `GET /api/v1/key` as shown above. To resolve errors: **Retry with exponential backoff.** Rate limits are transient; wait and retry rather than immediately re-sending. Honor the `Retry-After` header when present. **On free variants**, purchase at least {FREE_MODEL_CREDITS_THRESHOLD} credits to raise your daily limit, or switch to the paid variant of the model, which has no platform-level request cap. **For provider-side limits**, add [fallback models](/docs/guides/routing/model-fallbacks) or relax [provider routing preferences](/docs/guides/routing/provider-selection) so more providers are eligible to serve the request.

excerpts: A **subscription** is the recurring relationship between a customer and one of your [products](/docs/features/products).
It's created automatically whenever a customer checks out a product that has a recurring price, and it keeps generating orders on each renewal until the customer or you decide to end it.

**A customer subscribes.** When a customer completes a [checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session) for a product that has a recurring price, Polar creates a `subscription` and the first [order](/docs/features/orders).

**Polar renews it automatically.** At the end of each billing period, Polar advances the subscription to the next cycle and creates a new order, then attempts to charge the customer's default payment method. If the payment fails, the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar runs an automated [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments).

**Benefits stay in sync.** As long as the subscription is active or trialing, the customer keeps access to all the [benefits](/docs/features/benefits/introduction) attached to the product. When the subscription ends, those benefits are revoked.

Subscriptions > Recurring revenue on top of your products. A **subscription** is the recurring relationship between a customer and one of your [products](/docs/features/products). It's created automatically whenever a customer checks out a product that has a recurring price, and it keeps generating orders on each renewal until the customer or you decide to end it. How subscriptions work **A customer subscribes.** When a customer completes a [checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session) for a product that has a recurring price, Polar creates a `subscription` and the first [order](/docs/features/orders). **Polar renews it automatically.** At the end of each billing period, Polar advances the subscription to the next cycle and creates a new order, then attempts to charge the customer's default payment method. If the payment fails, the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar runs an automated [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments). **Benefits stay in sync.** As long as the subscription is active or trialing, the customer keeps access to all the [benefits](/docs/features/benefits/introduction) attached to the product. When the subscription ends, those benefits are revoked. **Customers self-serve from the portal.** The [Customer Portal](/docs/features/customer-portal/introduction) lets customers update their payment method, download invoices, cancel, and — if you allow it — change plans or manage seats. Recurring pricing Subscriptions are driven entirely by the way you price the underlying product. Recurring pricing is configured when you [create a product](/docs/features/products#pricing): **Billing interval.** Daily, weekly, monthly or yearly. **Interval count.** The number of units per cycle. Setting this to `2` with a `month` interval gives you "every 2 months". **Pricing type.** Fixed, pay-what-you-want, or free. Free recurring products are still modeled as subscriptions — they just never generate a payment. **Currency.** A product can have prices in multiple currencies; the subscription locks in the currency used at checkout. <Note> The billing interval and pricing type are fixed once a product is created. If you need a different interval (for example, a yearly plan next to a monthly one), create a separate product and show both at checkout. See [Products → Variants](/docs/features/products#variants). </Note> Renewal reminders For subscriptions on long billing cycles — six months or more — Polar emails the customer **7 days before the renewal date** to let them know an upcoming charge is coming. This helps with regulations (like the EU's Consumer Rights Directive) that require advance notice on long-interval renewals, and avoids surprise charges that often end in chargebacks. The threshold is six months, however it is expressed: yearly plans, monthly plans with an interval of 6 or more, weekly plans of 25 or more, and daily plans of 180 or more all get the reminder. Reminders are skipped for free subscriptions and for subscriptions already scheduled to cancel at period end. You can turn renewal reminders off under [**Settings → Customer notifications**](https://polar.sh/to/dashboard/settings) if you prefer to handle that communication yourself. Cancellation A subscription can end in one of two ways, both available to you and your customers: **Cancel at period end** — the subscription keeps working until `current_period_end`, then transitions to `canceled`. You can reverse this (uncancel) until the end date is reached. **Revoke immediately** — the subscription moves to `canceled` right away and benefits are revoked. This is irreversible. See [Managing subscriptions](/docs/features/subscriptions/manage) for how to perform these actions and everything else merchants can do from the dashboard or the API. Creating subscriptions There are two ways a subscription can come into existence: **Through checkout.** The default. Works for any paid recurring product. See [Checkout](/docs/features/checkout/session). **Through the API, for free recurring products only.** You can call [Create Subscription](/docs/api-reference/subscriptions/create-subscription) to subscribe an existing customer to a free product — no order, no email, no charge. This is useful for freemium onboarding flows where you want every signup to have a subscription tied to it from day one. Paid products always go through checkout so that Polar can collect and validate the payment method. Next steps <CardGroup cols={2}> <Card title="Managing subscriptions" icon="sliders" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/manage"> Change plans, seats, trials, billing dates, cancel or revoke — from the dashboard or the API. </Card> <Card title="Proration" icon="scale-balanced" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/proration"> Control how the price difference is handled when a subscription is upgraded or downgraded. </Card> <Card title="Recovering failed payments" icon="credit-card" href="/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments"> How Polar retries failed renewals and when benefits are revoked. </Card> <Card title="Subscriptions API" icon="code" href="/docs/api-reference/subscriptions/list-subscriptions"> List, create, update, and revoke subscriptions programmatically. </Card> </CardGroup> FAQ <AccordionGroup> <Accordion title="What's the difference between a subscription and a product?"> A product is the thing you're selling — name, description, benefits, pricing. A subscription is one specific customer's ongoing relationship with that product. Polar treats one-time purchases and recurring subscriptions as the same kind of object (both are "products"); the only difference is whether the price is recurring. See [Products](/docs/features/products) for the full model. </Accordion> <Accordion title="Can a customer have more than one active subscription?"> By default, no — a customer can only have one active subscription per organization at a time. This keeps the common case simple. If your product genuinely needs multiple parallel subscriptions per customer, you can opt in under **Organization Settings → Subscriptions** by toggling on **Allow multiple subscriptions**. </Accordion> <Accordion title="When is a customer actually charged?"> At the end of each billing cycle. When a subscription renews, Polar advances the cycle, creates a new order with tax and any applicable discount, and charges the customer's default payment method. If the charge fails the subscription moves to `past_due` and Polar starts the [payment recovery flow](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments). The first charge happens at checkout (or when the [trial](/docs/features/subscriptions/trials) ends, if one is configured). </Accordion> <Accordion title="Can I change the price of an existing subscription?"> Not the amount on an existing subscription directly — subscriptions lock in the price they were created with so existing subscribers aren't surprised by changes. If you update the price on a product, the change applies only to **new** subscriptions. To move an existing subscriber to different pricing, either create a new product and run an [update to switch them to it](/docs/features/subscriptions/manage#change-the-plan), or ask them to change plans themselves from the Customer Portal. </Accordion> <Accordion title="What happens to benefits when a subscription is canceled?"> Benefits are tied to the subscription's status, not to the cancellation action itself: If you **cancel at period end**, the customer keeps their benefits until `current_period_end` — they paid for that period. If you **revoke immediately**, the subscription becomes `canceled` right away and all benefits are revoked. If a renewal payment can't be recovered after Polar's retries, the subscription moves to `unpaid` and benefits are revoked the same way as a revoke — subject to the optional [grace period](/docs/features/subscriptions/failed-payments#benefit-revocation-grace-period) you can configure on your organization. </Accordion> </AccordionGroup>

content.1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_a:
The comparison set is not one market. It contains four buying motions with different economic owners.

| ICP | Representative products and evidence | Primary payer | What the payer is buying |
|---|---|---|---|
| Personal learner, researcher, freelancer | Heptabase targets anyone building a lifelong knowledge base at **$8.99/month** for Pro; Craft Plus is **$8 monthly or $6.40 yearly** for one account. [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[0]] [21] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[1]] [9] | Individual user | Private thinking space, portability, search, and low-friction AI |
| Small collaborative team | Miro Starter is **$8/member/month billed yearly** and Figma Professional has Full, Dev, and Collab seats at **$16, $12, and $3/month** respectively. [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[2]] [15] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[3]] [17] | Team lead, design lead, or department budget | Shared canvas, permissions, collaboration, and workflow continuity |
| Studio or agency operator team | Productive prices by users and requires at least **3 seats**; Scoro combines apps at **EUR15/user/month** and requires at least **5 seats**. [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[4]] [19] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[5]] [12] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[5]] [12] | Founder, operations lead, finance lead, or agency budget | Utilization, margin, resource allocation, approvals, billing, and control |
| Client-reporting agency | AgencyAnalytics charges **$20/client/month** and includes staff and client users. [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[6]] [7] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[6]] [7] | Agency owner or account-services budget | Client-facing reporting, white label, portals, and client capacity |
| AI-heavy individual or team | Motion charges **$19/seat/month** for Pro AI and **$29/seat/month** for Business AI; Cursor charges **$20/month** for Pro and **$40/user/month** for Teams. [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[7]] [6] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[7]] [6] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[8]] [4] | Individual for personal AI; company for shared context and administration | Time saved, model access, agent execution, and team governance |

The key mechanism is that the buyer changes when the product crosses from personal output to shared liability. A freelancer can self-serve a $10-$20 subscription. An agency owner pays when the system controls billable time, staffing, client commitments, and cash collection. That is why Productive and Scoro sell operations as a per-user system, while AgencyAnalytics can price per client: the measurable value unit differs.

Notion is the clearest personal-to-team case. Its Free plan is positioned for individuals, Plus for small teams and professionals, and Business for growing businesses; paid plans charge per member, while guests are free but restricted to invited pages. [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[9]] [22] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[9]] [22] [1_who_pays_personal_team_studio_agency_and_ai_buyers[9]] [22] This reveals a useful Orch pattern: personal adoption should not require a sales conversation, but shared ownership, roles, and operational data should move into a company-paid workspace.

The recommendation is therefore not one universal SKU. Let a person own a personal workspace and optionally create or join a team workspace. The team or organization owns the bill, the AI wallet, the member roster, and the operational records. A user identity should be a member of those scopes, not the scope itself.

The pattern is functional free, then paid scale. Miro gives a real whiteboard but limits editable boards. Craft gives usable content but limits blocks, history, and shared spaces. Clockify and Harvest let a person track time before charging for users, projects, approvals, invoices, and team reporting. These are conversion gates because they appear at the point where the user has created a repeatable workflow and now needs scale.

Miro is a useful case study for Orch. Its free plan permits unlimited members but only three editable boards, while paid tiers add unlimited or private boards and AI credits. [2_published_canvas_and_time_tracking_price_anchors[0]] [15] [2_published_canvas_and_time_tracking_price_anchors[0]] [15] The mechanism is not merely scarcity: the free user can experience the core canvas, but collaboration and recurring AI use create a natural upgrade. Orch should copy that mechanism, not necessarily the exact board count.

The recommended canvas free tier is one useful personal workspace with a high enough content allowance to demonstrate the product. If performance requires a content cap, make it visible, server-enforced, and materially above the activation threshold. A **200-node cap on Pro** is likely a weak or decorative promise: Craft already publishes 1,500 free blocks, while Notion allows an individual user to add as many pages and blocks as desired on Free. [2_published_canvas_and_time_tracking_price_anchors[3]] [9] [2_published_canvas_and_time_tracking_price_anchors[8]] [22] Use a board, workspace, history, export, or collaboration boundary only when it corresponds to a real cost or value event.

[4_ai_packaging_included_quotas_credits_model_tiers_and_arrears[1]] [6] [4_ai_packaging_included_quotas_credits_model_tiers_and_arrears[1]] [6] Cursor makes the allowance explicit but permits on-demand usage billed in arrears after the included amount. [4_ai_packaging_included_quotas_credits_model_tiers_and_arrears[3]] [4] The first model is easier to budget; the second captures power-user willingness to pay but requires spend controls and clear consent.

Notion demonstrates a third mechanism: standard AI is part of the workspace experience, while Custom Agents and additional usage draw from a shared workspace credit balance. [4_ai_packaging_included_quotas_credits_model_tiers_and_arrears[0]] [22] This is closer to Orch's likely economics because a team may want one shared pool for research, synthesis, and automation rather than a hard per-user quota.

The proposed "unlimited AI conversations" is safe only if it means unlimited low-cost conversational turns subject to fair use, not unlimited premium model calls, web research, long-context synthesis, OCR, or agent execution. Define a user-facing AI credit as a weighted action, not a raw token. Include a monthly pool for ordinary chat, show remaining balance, reserve premium models for metered credits, and require explicit auto-top-up or admin approval for overage.
content.5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_worksp:
Stripe's freemium guidance is directly applicable: the free plan should put the core job front and center, solve a real need, and reserve better, faster, or larger-scale execution for paid plans. It identifies usage limits such as storage, seats, and projects, feature gates such as automation, integrations, and admin controls, and experience gates such as speed, support, and customization. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[0]] [10] It also warns that giving away too much cannibalizes paid tiers while giving away too little prevents users from becoming invested. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[0]] [10] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[0]] [10]

| Gate type | Evidence in the market | Orch recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Content scale | Miro limits Free to 3 editable boards; Craft Free to 1,500 blocks and 7-day history. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[1]] [15] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[2]] [9] | Use a real storage or history boundary only if it protects cost or creates a clear upgrade moment |
| Collaboration scale | Harvest Free has 1 seat and 2 projects; Clockify Free supports up to 5 users. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[3]] [8] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[4]] [11] | Allow a person to adopt alone; charge when shared work, approvals, or team reporting matter |
| Product scale | Linear Free has unlimited members but only 2 teams and 250 issues; Notion Free gives an individual unlimited pages and blocks but limits blocks when multiple members use the workspace. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[5]] [14] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[6]] [22] | Keep identity-level adoption open, then gate team scope, operational history, roles, and admin |
| Cost-to-serve | Notion credits, Miro credits, Heptabase credits, Motion credits, and Cursor included usage all expose an AI allowance or overage boundary. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[6]] [22] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[1]] [15] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[7]] [21] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[8]] [6] [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[9]] [4] | Meter expensive AI actions; do not meter ordinary navigation, basic notes, or time-entry capture |

The conversion mechanism is a bottleneck that arrives after value. A user who has created a personal knowledge system should not be blocked by an arbitrary node count before understanding Orch. A team that needs approvals, resource allocation, client billing, or shared AI context should encounter a meaningful paywall because those features create operational and support costs.

The personal-workspace-plus-team pattern should work as follows. Every account gets a personal workspace. A user can create a team workspace or accept an invitation. The team workspace owns members, roles, data retention, AI budget, integrations, and invoices. Guests can be free or low-cost if they are restricted to invited canvases or client views, as Notion does for guests. [5_freemium_gates_and_the_personal_workspace_plus_team_pattern[6]] [22]

This design also prevents a common pricing trap: charging a solo user for a team feature before there is a team, while allowing a large agency to hide behind one paid identity. The first editor can be free or low-cost; the moment the organization needs multiple editors, operational controls, or pooled AI, billing moves to the workspace.

Polar is attractive for an early AI SaaS because it combines billing and compliance around usage events. Its homepage describes live meters for tokens, API calls, compute, and storage; recurring plans with proration; seats; prepaid balances; and usage settling at the end of the cycle. [6_polar_sh_versus_stripe_for_b2b_saas_billing[0]] [28] [6_polar_sh_versus_stripe_for_b2b_saas_billing[0]] [28] That reduces the amount of finance infrastructure Orch must build before testing AI monetization.

Stripe is the better fit when Orch expects complex enterprise procurement, multiple payment methods, invoicing, negotiated contracts, or a large existing Stripe ecosystem. Stripe's entitlement model is especially useful as a conceptual boundary even if Orch uses Polar: product plans should map to features, but application code should decide whether the feature belongs to a user, team, workspace, organization, or client account. [6_polar_sh_versus_stripe_for_b2b_saas_billing[3]] [1]

The recommendation is Polar-first for a self-serve global beta if the team accepts Merchant of Record economics and Polar's product surface. Use Stripe when enterprise billing, tax ownership, invoicing, or extensibility outweighs implementation speed. Do not run Polar for subscriptions and Stripe separately for AI usage without a single internal ledger. The customer should see one plan, one balance, one invoice explanation, and one entitlement state.

| SKU | Recommended price band | Leave free or include | Gate or meter |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Personal Free | $0 | One personal workspace, core canvas, basic notes, basic time capture, limited sharing, and a small monthly allowance of low-cost AI | Gate private history, exports at scale, advanced integrations, premium models, and agent actions |

| Team | **$15-$20 per active editor/month**, with a 3-seat minimum or a $39-$59 workspace base | Shared canvases, roles, team activity, pooled standard AI, and basic approvals | Gate advanced roles, audit, resourcing, automations, SSO, and premium AI pool size |
| Agency | **$25-$40 per active operator/month**, or roughly $199-$399 per workspace base including a small operator bundle | Resourcing, utilization, budgets, profitability, approvals, rate cards, billing, client views, and pooled AI controls | Meter client-account scale, premium automations, deep integrations, and high-volume AI; keep client viewers free or low-cost |
| AI add-on | **$10-$20/user/month** standard or **$49-$199/workspace/month** pooled credits | Standard chat and a base allowance already included in paid plans | Charge weighted credits for premium models, agent runs, research, document parsing, and overage |
| Enterprise | Custom annual contract | SSO, SCIM, audit, data controls, procurement, support, and negotiated usage | Contracted seats, service levels, retention, and committed AI spend |

These are recommended launch bands, not claims about a competitor's exact price. They are anchored by the market: Miro Business is $20 per member, Notion Business is $20 per member, Motion Pro AI is $19 per seat, Cursor Pro is $20, and the agency products move from Productive's $10 starting point and Scoro's EUR15 starting point into higher tiers as controls and modules accumulate. ### Decision on the proposed $19 all-in Pro

Keep the $19 price, but change the contract. It should be Personal Pro for one paying owner, or a workspace base that includes only a small number of paid editors. The promise of 5 teams and 20 members is acceptable only if most of those people are viewers, guests, or non-billable collaborators with explicit restrictions. It is not acceptable as 20 full agency operators with unlimited operations and AI.

Remove the phrase "unlimited AI conversations" from the commercial promise. Replace it with "unlimited standard chat subject to fair use, plus X AI credits for premium actions." OpenRouter returns token counts, credit cost, reasoning and cache data with responses, and its limits distinguish account balance, per-key caps, and free-model request ceilings. [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[6]] [26] [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[6]] [26] [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[7]] [29] A backend that pays those costs while exposing no wallet, cap, or overage path has an uncapped liability.

Treat 200 canvas nodes as an implementation limit, not the headline value of Pro. If the limit is needed for performance, enforce it server-side and explain the reason. Otherwise, use a meaningful collaboration or history gate. The market evidence suggests that users understand boards, projects, seats, reports, and AI credits better than an arbitrary node number. [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[0]] [15] [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[8]] [9] [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[9]] [8]

### Entitlement model and failure prevention

Use four separate records:

1. **Billing account**: customer identity, payment provider IDs, tax status, invoices, and subscription status.
2. **Workspace or organization**: the scope that owns plan, seats, AI wallet, data, integrations, and operational features.
3. **Membership**: user, role, seat type, team membership, guest status, and active/deactivated state.
4. **Usage and limits**: append-only AI ledger, content counters, seat counters, client counters, and feature checks.

The common broken Polar pattern is a user-scoped subscription granting a team-scoped feature. Fix it by attaching the subscription to a workspace or organization and deriving user access from membership and role. Polar's subscription lifecycle describes benefits attached to the subscription, while Stripe's entitlement model describes feature grant and revocation; neither removes the need for Orch to model scope correctly. [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[10]] [13] [7_recommended_orch_sku_ladder_free_surface_and_metering[11]] [1]

The second broken pattern is advertising member, node, or block limits that are checked only in the front end. Check every create, invite, upload, export, background job, and API mutation, with an idempotent counter or ledger. The third is calling AI unlimited while silently paying OpenRouter credits. Show usage, enforce per-key and workspace budgets, set hard or soft caps, and require an explicit top-up for overage. OpenRouter's own documentation exposes usage and cost data precisely so applications can monitor consumption and limits. content.synthesis:
The four product families differ along mechanism, scope, trade-off, and time horizon.

| Family | Monetization mechanism | Entitlement scope | Main trade-off | Orch implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Canvas | Per seat, seat type, individual subscription, or fixed small-team bundle | Board, document, account, or workspace | Low entry price creates adoption, but collaboration and AI must expand revenue | Make the personal canvas generous; monetize shared operations and scale |
| Time tracking | Per seat with free user/project limits | User, team, project, approval, and billing scope | Basic capture is cheap; administration and profitability are valuable | Keep basic tracking free; charge for approvals, billable rates, and reporting |
| Agency OS | Per user, module, client, or custom contract | Organization, operator, client, and financial workflow | Higher ACV supports support and implementation, but sales cycles are longer | Separate Agency SKU and sell measurable delivery economics |
| AI workspace | Included quota, credits, model tiers, or arrears | User allowance, workspace pool, provider key, and model class | Unlimited language creates unpredictable cost and abuse | Bundle ordinary chat, meter expensive actions, and make budgets visible |

The non-obvious tension is between Linear and Clockify. Linear leaves members unlimited but caps teams and issues, while Clockify caps free users and then charges seats. [synthesis[0]] [14] [synthesis[1]] [11] One optimizes for broad product adoption and usage scarcity; the other optimizes for a clear seat conversion. Orch should combine them: allow identity and personal adoption broadly, but enforce workspace, operational, and AI scale where value and cost rise.

A second tension is between Craft's fixed Team bundle and Figma's role-based seats. Craft packages up to 10 Plus accounts for $50/month, while Figma differentiates Full, Dev, and Collab seats. [synthesis[2]] [9] [synthesis[3]] [17] Fixed bundles reduce choice friction for small studios; role-based seats improve price fairness at scale. Start with a simple Team plan, then add viewer, collaborator, operator, and admin roles only when customer behavior proves the need.

The final divergence is Polar versus Stripe. Polar compresses Merchant of Record, tax, usage metering, and billing into a faster route to global self-serve. Stripe exposes strong building blocks for usage, tax, and entitlements, but leaves Orch more responsibility for the complete commercial architecture. [synthesis[4]] [28] [synthesis[5]] [2] [synthesis[6]] [1] [synthesis[7]] [27] The durable strategy is provider-agnostic entitlements and an internal usage ledger. Then billing infrastructure can change without rewriting the product's definition of who owns a team, what a seat is, or what an AI credit costs.

The launch decision is therefore: **ship Personal Free, Personal Pro at $19 monthly, Team at $15-$20 per active editor, Agency at $25-$40 per operator or a workspace base, and a transparent AI credit add-on.** The $19 plan is a compelling wedge when it buys one person's complete workflow. It becomes a margin and entitlement failure when it quietly promises 20 full agency users and unlimited provider-funded AI.
